Brave Help Guide

The official Brave help documentation, gathered into one document

2026-08-02

Brave Help Guide

This guide gathers the official Brave help documentation, as it stood on 2 August 2026.

How this was gathered, and why that is worth saying. Brave’s rendered help pages refuse automated reading. Every one of them answered with a refusal, and they did so even when asked exactly as an ordinary web browser asks. But Brave’s own publishing system offers the same articles through a listing, and that listing answered without complaint. The text here is Brave’s, complete, taken from Brave: title, section and body exactly as published. All 241 articles arrived carrying their text.

The arrangement is Brave’s own. The categories are the section names Brave files its articles under, each preceded by the platform it belongs to. That prefix is not decoration: Brave uses the same six section names – Installing Brave, Settings Management, Browsing basics, Brave Features, Privacy and Security and New Tab Page – under Desktop, Android and iOS alike. Installing Brave on a phone is not installing it on a desktop, and a guide that ran the two together would send a reader looking for buttons that are not there.

Sections holding a single article have been folded into Miscellaneous, since a category of one is not a category.

What was left out. Brave keeps a Japanese help centre inside its English tree, and 14 articles there are written in Japanese. Brave’s own note on that section says it is being migrated to a Japanese help centre and will be removed once that is done. This collection keeps one language per volume, so those are not here.

Also outside this guide, by the standing conventions of this collection: Brave’s community forum, which is users talking to one another rather than Brave’s own writing, and the developer documentation.

Cross-references between articles have been resolved into links within this document, by Brave’s own article identifiers, so following a “see also” never leaves the file. Illustrations do not survive the conversion.

Android Browser: Privacy and Security

How do I check if a site’s connection is secure?

To see whether a website is safe to visit, you can check for security info about the site. Brave will alert you if you can’t visit the site safely or privately.

  1. In Brave, open a page.
  2. To check a site’s security, to the left of the web address, look at the security status:
  •  Secure
  •  Not secure
  •  Dangerous

To see the site’s details and permissions, select the icon. You’ll see a summary of how private Brave thinks the connection is.

What each security symbol means

These symbols let you know how safe it is to visit and use a site. They tell you if a site has a security certificate, if Brave trusts that certificate, and if Brave has a private connection with a site.

 Secure

Information you send or get through the site is private.

Even if you see this icon, always be careful when sharing private information. Look at the address bar to make sure you’re on the site you want to visit.

 Not secure

The site isn’t using a private connection. Someone might be able to see or change the information you send or get through this site. 

On some sites, you can visit a more secure version of the page:

  1. Select the address bar.
  2. Delete http://, and enter https:// instead.

If that doesn’t work, contact the site owner to ask that they secure the site and your data with HTTPS.

 Dangerous

We suggest you don’t enter any private or personal information on this page. If possible, don’t use the site.

Not secure: Proceed with caution. Something is severely wrong with the privacy of this site’s connection. Someone might be able to see the information you send or get through this site.

You might see a “Login not secure” or “Payment not secure” message.

Dangerous: Avoid this site. If you see a full-page red warning screen, the site has been flagged as unsafe. Using the site will likely put your private information at risk.

Fix “Your connection is not private” error

If you see a full-page error message saying “Your connection is not private,” then there’s a problem with the site, the network, or your device. 

What a security certificate is

When you go to a site that uses HTTPS (connection security), the website’s server uses a certificate to prove the website’s identity to browsers, like Brave. Anyone can create a certificate claiming to be whatever website they want.

To help you stay on safe on the web, Brave requires websites to use certificates from trusted organizations.

What are lookalike URLs?

If you see this message, Brave thinks that the website address in the address bar may be for a different site than the one you intended to visit.

There are three reasons why you might see this message:

  • The URL looks similar to a site that you visit frequently.
  • The URL appears to be trying to trick you with an address that is slightly modified from a well-known site.
  • The URL is slightly different from one in your browsing history.

If you think this message appeared as a mistake, and you know the URL is accurate, you can click Yes, continue to dismiss the message and proceed.

The list of safe sites and lookalike rules is maintained by the Chrome team. You can find more information about this functionality in their technical documentation, including how site owners can report false positives.

What does brave remove from the Chromium engine?

(Note that this page is a work in progress and may be updated frequently)

Brave for desktop is built on top of the open-source Chromium project. We add features on top of what is already there and we also remove features or pieces of the code. These deviations we make that touch the core Chromium code are done via patching.

Chromium is not the same as Google Chrome. For some differences, see https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/master/docs/chromium_browser_vs_google_chrome.md.

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#how-it-works)How it works

If you wanted to do an audit of the code, you would start with the brave-browser repository. Our wiki has instructions about what steps need to be done to perform a build after cloning the source

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#chromium-source-is-fetched)Chromium source is fetched

The gclient utility (part of depot tools) will fetch the official Chromium source code. The tag that is fetched is captured in our package.json(for example,70.0.3538.35). All of the source code will be downloaded into the./src/folder

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#brave-code-is-fetched)Brave code is fetched

As part of the setup process, we also fetch our own code. The brave-core repository has the code that makes the browser Brave. The branch that should be checked out is also contained in that package.json. There is also a DEPS file in brave-core that pulls in sub-dependencies (such as the brave-extension)

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#hooks-are-run)Hooks are run

After the gclient sync runs and fetches all the code (including brave-core), the hooks are run. One of the hooks that runs applies the patches (which you can see here) that are contained in brave-core. If you’d like to know more details about HOW the patching works, you can view our patching wiki page.

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#what-chromium-features-are-removed-for-privacysecurity-reasons)What Chromium features are removed for privacy/security reasons?

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#services--features-we-disable-entirely)Services & Features We Disable Entirely
  • Google accounts integration (“GAIA”) is disabled
  • All features that send data to Google are removed from settings
  • DNS prefetching is disabled
  • Chrome Google URL Tracker is disabled
  • Domain service reliability is disabled
  • Inline extensions are disabled
  • Background sync is disabled
  • Hyperlinkpingattribute is disabled
  • Disable Battery API
  • Disable WebBluetooth API
  • WebRTC debug log uploading is disabled
  • Uploading settings after resetting profile is disabled
  • Retrieving OEM default settings after resetting profile is disabled
  • Tracing crash log uploading is disabled
  • Google Cloud Messaging is disabled
  • Firebase Cloud Messaging is disabled
  • Push client channel updates are disabled
  • Network time tracker is disabled
  • Google-assisted address normalization is disabled
  • Specific features are disabled on startup via the CLI (search fordisabled_features)
  • Remove dl.google.com repository from Linux packages
  • Disable metrics reporting
  • Disable Lookalike URLs Navigation Suggestions
  • Disable Reporting Observers and Reporting API
  • Disable Scroll To Text Fragment

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#services-we-proxy-through-brave-servers)Services We Proxy Through Brave Servers

Google does not receive any information about which client is performing these requests (not even your IP address).

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#modified-features-and-functionality)Modified Features and Functionality
  • Cookies are given a maximum lifetime of 7 days for cookies set through Javascript and 6 months for cookies set through HTTP
  • Referrer values are capped tostrict-origin-when-cross-originand can only be tightened by referrer policy, not weakened. In addition, cross-origin requests from a.onionservice have an emptyRefererheader and anull``Originheader just like the Tor Browser.
  • Media Router (Chromecast) is disabled by default on Desktop. You can turn it on by toggling the switch in brave://settings.
  • Download protection remote lookups omit URLs and filenames ().
  • Have StorageManager.estimate report a fixed value( issue #11543)
  • Many features have randomness added or values generalized as a defense against fingerprinting, including:
    • Canvas readback methods
    • User Agent, follow ups in issues #12097, #12638, #14740
    • enumerateDevices
    • Web Audio Serialization
    • WebGL Debug
    • Plugins
    • hardwareConcurrency
    • deviceMemory
  • The list of hostnames with pinned CA certificates is replaced with a Brave-specific one.
  • Restore gesture requirement for async clipboard write access
https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#comments)Comments

Some of the above (along with other issues) were previously tracked in .

You may notice some requests to Google domains. Some of these, such asclients*.google.com and update.googleapis.com are needed to check for extension updates if you installed extensions.

https://github.com/brave/brave-browser/wiki/Deviations-from-Chromium-(features-we-disable-or-remove#how-does-brave-compare-to-ungoogled-chromium)How does Brave compare to ungoogled-chromium?

Description of ungoogled-chromium, per their GitHub page:

ungoogled-chromium is Google Chromium, sans integration with Google. It also features some tweaks to enhance privacy, control, and transparency(almost all of which require manual activation or enabling).

We have an issue captured for pulling in relevant patches from theungoogled-chromiumproject. Theungoogled-chromiumproject similarly has an issue captured where they mention pulling in patches from Brave.

What is a Private Window Android?

A private window in Brave prevents Internet browsing history, form data, cookies and site data from being saved once you close the window. However, bookmarks saved from private windows are saved for regular windows too.

Private browsing stops browsers from saving browsing activity beyond the current session; however, you activity may still be visible to:

  • Certain websites you visit (this includes the ads and resources used on those sites)
  • The Owner/Administrator of your network
  • Your internet service provider (ISP)

Note that some cookies and site data may be saved for the session, but will not be remembered when the browser is closed. Downloads and bookmarks are still saved even after closing a private window.

You can learn more about browsing with Private Windows and Tor Connectivity below.

Do Private Windows Make Me Anonymous?

What is P3A in Brave?

Introduction

At Brave, we want our browser not only to provide the best protection against the surveillance economy, but to be the very best way to experience the web.  We rely extensively on community feedback to make sure that the product provides the most vital features and is as reliable as it can possibly be. Sometimes, however, this simply is not enough to make sure we are providing the best experience to as many users as possible.  Many people simply don’t have time to provide feedback, and there are many questions left unanswered. Do people make it through onboarding, or do we need to make it shorter? Are people using Brave Rewards? Are people using sync and if so, on how many devices? How many people still need to download important browser updates?  

In an ordinary software company, these questions would be answered by using one of dozens of third-party analytics services. But the way such services operate would mean that Brave users could be individually identified and tracked, by a third party, and in some cases that behavior would be aggregated with other tracked behavior from the ad/tracker ecosystem for the benefit of the third party alone. None of this would be remotely acceptable to Brave given our commitment to user privacy. 

We believe that completely private product analytics are the most effective way for us to make Brave the best it can be — by providing us with insights into how the various features of the product are actually being used, so we can shape the product to better match the needs of our users.  As always, our code is open source and available for third-party audits and verification.

How P3A Works

Privacy is our first value. We really, genuinely don’t want to know anything about you individually, or to know anything that could be used to track you. That means that we need to approach product analytics very differently from most other companies. We’ve built a completely private system which we’re calling Privacy-Preserving Product Analytics, or P3A for short. This project goes well beyond industry norms and GDPR requirements when it comes to privacy preservation. Here are the mechanics:

  • P3A doesn’t collect any personal information. Nothing that could identify you, and nothing sensitive like your browser history, search queries, etc.
  • Every so often, in the background, the browser sends reports containing simple, non-identifying information on product feature usage. These are essentially automatically-delivered answers to specific questions defined by Brave.
  • All answers are safeguarded by STAR, an award-winning (CCS ‘22) cryptographic telemetry system. STAR guarantees that Brave only accesses an answer if several users reported the same one, thus providing “anonymity through a crowd” and preventing linkability between individual reports.
  • We send some attributes (such as the browser version) with each P3A answer. These attributes are also cryptographically protected by STAR and we are only able to access attribute information on an answer if several users reported the same attribute for that answer. This is to ensure that we don’t learn anything about individual users even via metadata.
  • We limit overlapping questions as well as questions that span collection periods as a further protection against report linkage.
  • All the “questions” we ask of the browser (the measurements collected) will be posted publicly in human-readable form.  You can find the current list here. 
  • You can turn P3A off at any time in the “Privacy and Security” section of the browser preferences.
  • All the P3A code will be open source (as is all our code except anti-fraud server-side code) — you can always check that your browser is only sharing the specific things we promise.

This system is designed so that we, Brave, are unable to associate any particular response with any other, so we do not have sufficient information to link together any particular user’s “answers”. Instead, each response is an independent data point.

You can see the full list of questions and attributes on our Github here:  

Data Retention

Log level records are automatically deleted from our servers within 30 days.  Note that these log-level records will not contain IP addresses or exact timing information.  Our anonymized summaries of the data are intended to be kept indefinitely.

Privacy Policy

Brave’s privacy policy can be found here: https://brave.com/privacy/ 

Conclusion

Most of the software you use includes some sort of product analytics, or usage data collection, as does every major browser. And for good reason — knowing which features are resonating and which need work is an important part of making software that’s a pleasure to use. We’ve been cautious about building analytics because we knew we had to get it exactly right. Some other browsers collect thousands of measurements along with a substantial amount of information about what you’ve searched for and which sites you visited. None of the commercial analytics products we’ve seen come anywhere close to our privacy standards. Building this ourselves took a lot longer than using an existing system, but we think that’s time well spent. We hope you agree.

What is the Web Discovery Project in Brave?

The Web Discovery Project is a privacy-preserving way for you to contribute to the growth and independence of Brave Search. If you opt in, you’ll contribute some anonymous data about searches and web page visits made within the Brave Browser (including pages arrived at via some, but not all, other search engines). This data helps build the Brave Search independent index, and ensure we show relevant results to your search queries and support more relevant experiences with Brave products and services.By “data” we mean search queries, search result clicks, the URLs of pages visited in the browser, time spent on those pages, and some metadata about the pages themselves.

The Web Discovery Project runs in the background, so it requires no effort on the part of contributors. Data contributed cannot be linked back to whoever contributed it, or grouped together, which prevents deanonymization attempts. Opt out at any time.

💡To disable P3A in Android: Settings --> Brave Shields & Privacy --> Web Discovery Project

Why we built the Web Discovery Project

Providing relevant search results is essential to building a search engine people want to use. It’s how we create a private search engine that still competes with big tech on quality and completeness. To ensure search results are as relevant as possible, Brave needs to understand some key things, including:

  • How closely search results match the search keywords (matching to exact words, parts of words, or synonyms)
  • How recent searches are for those keywords
  • How often a search result is clicked for a given keyword
  • How popular search keywords are
  • What pages are popular or novel
  • Which sites only allow crawling by the Google search bot

Ensuring relevance also means reducing the “noise” from web content that makes a search less relevant. For example, if you search for “Europe weather” and see results relating to European history or European business, you would say the results are less relevant to your query. Learning through the Web Discovery Project enables Brave Search to filter this noise out, but in a privacy-preserving way. Making search more relevant shouldn’t come at the expense of your online privacy.

Context

Most search providers—like Google and Microsoft—collect data about your search behavior, both in the search engine and the browser (like Chrome or Edge). This data includes your queries, what search results you click, the URLs of the pages you visit, time spent on those pages, and metadata (such as page title, content-type, etc) about the pages themselves. Other, non-independent search engines (like DuckDuckGo) don’t necessarily collect data themselves. But they still rely on this kind of collection via their dependence on other big tech indexes (like Bing). And this data can—and often is—associated with you personally.

Search providers collect this kind of data to continuously grow their indexes—the list of billions of web pages they draw from to deliver results—and ensure results are relevant and never stale. This collection isn’t inherently bad. But it’s shortcomings become apparent when you look at Brave’s alternative way:

  • The Web Discovery Project allows you to contribute anonymous, generalized data.
  • The Web Discovery Project is designed to prevent us from associating this data with you. This means there’s no data for Brave to sell to advertisers, or lose to theft or hacking, allowing us to promise through technology rather than words.
  • Brave’s Web Discovery Project is opt-in only, and totally transparent.

The protection of unlinkability

Brave doesn’t follow the sneaky practices of other big tech search engines. The Web Discovery Project is opt-in, and the data collected under the Web Discovery Project has specific protections to ensure anonymity. In addition to these protections, the Web Discovery Project adheres to the principle of “unlinkability.” This means we do not link data to you, your browser, or your device. Brave Search has no concept of a user or session ID, which prevents record linkability. Further, the Web Discovery Project includes multiple protections to prevent websites or searches specific to you, or that include personal or sensitive information, from inclusion.

What keywords are being searched most often? What websites do those keywords lead to? How are those websites interacted with? These kinds of directional questions help Brave Search navigate the world of available web pages, and separate signal from noise. And this, in turn, helps us understand the parts of the web worth indexing for users.

What the Web Discovery Project collects, how, and why

If you opt-in to the Web Discovery Project, your browser will process the following data on your device, and securely send it to Brave’s servers:

  • A fraction of the addresses (URLs) of the web pages visited in the Brave Browser, along with engagement metrics (how much time is spent on the page)
  • A fraction of the queries (e.g. “New York weather today”) conducted in some search engines (outside of Brave Search) within the Brave Browser, along with the associated click on a result (if any)
  • Metadata of those visited pages (e.g. if the page contains a video, info about page author or owner, page title, etc.), never the content of the page itself.
  • For a complete list, check out Brave’s GitHub repo

With this data, Brave can learn (in a private, unlinkable way) things like how many visits to a website (e.g. Wikipedia) lasted longer than 20 seconds, or how many times a given query (e.g. “What is Wikipedia?”) led a user to click through to that website. This calibrates Brave Search to know a website is legitimate, and that users find the content valuable. This, in turn, allows the search engine to understand result relevance, and to serve pages with higher relevance at the top of search results.

This data does not allow Brave to know things like associated queries (e.g. other queries conducted by people who searched “What is Wikipedia?”) or the other websites visited. And it of course tells us nothing that would allow us to link the data to an individual or their device.

Is there external validation of the Web Discovery Project methodology?

The Web Discovery Project methodology is based on an earlier methodology (known as “Human Web”) created by Cliqz in 2016. It has been in production since then, with no known breakage. Brave ported the methodology to the Brave Browser, and expanded with additional systems to ensure privacy, such as using n-out-of-k secret sharing schemes, as well as conducting further privacy and security reviews. For external audits, a HackerOne program is in place.

Can I opt-out of the Web Discovery Project, even after I opt-in?

By default, all users are opted out of the Web Discovery Project. If you’ve chosen to opt in, you can opt out again at any time. Whatever you choose—opt in or opt out—your experience in Brave or Brave Search will not change.

To opt out, open a new tab in the Brave browser and click Settings. Scroll to “Web Discovery Project,” and toggle this setting off.

What happens to the data I contribute? Can it be removed?

No. Because of the principle of record-unlinkability, we have no way of determining which data you contributed (this would violate Brave’s privacy policy, and our own ethics). Data sent to Brave enters a common pool, and is indistinguishable from data contributed by other people or devices. We can’t remove data that isn’t associated with you in the first place.

Is there a data retention policy?

Web Discover Project data is not personal data as defined under laws like the EU General Data Protection Regulation. It cannot be linked to any one individual or their devices, or be used to single out individuals. While there’s no legal obligation to determine a retention period for this kind of non-personal data, we have decided to erase data one year after it’s collected.

Is there a performance impact to opting in to the Web Discovery Project?

The Web Discovery Project is lightweight and runs only in the background. There should be no noticeable impact on browsing speed, page-rendering speed, or other similar metrics. However, there may be some small (but likely unnoticeable) overhead in the form of extra CPU and bandwidth consumed. Note that the Web Discover Project only runs on desktop devices, so there is no impact on mobile data plans. If you notice performance issues, please notify us immediately.

Is the Web Discovery Project a crawler?

In a way, yes. The Web Discovery Project processes fetch jobs from Brave’s web crawler. Every few seconds or minutes, the browser might be instructed to fetch a webpage and send the HTML back to Brave. However, this fetching has no impact on your browsing history or cookies—it’s done as a private fetch API call. For extra safety, the fetch job domains are pre-selected from a small set of innocuous and reputable domains.

How does the Web Discovery Project handle authenticated pages or pages with personal info?

All URLs sent must be publicly available—that is, they must have the same content regardless of who is contributing them. This can only be true if the pages are not behind a log-in, individual session, or other authentication. All URLs sent must have been visited by at least 20 different people, which establishes a distributed quorum similar to k-anonymity.

Additionally, there are a variety of heuristics applied to rule out URLs that encode access i.e. capability URLs (such as shared docs, Dropbox links, invoice links, etc). By design, none of these URLs are sent. And, even if they somehow were, the record-unlinkability protocol means no one with access to the data could recover other URLs from the same origin, or associate any data with anyone.

The above protections also apply to search queries. Any query containing what appears to be personal data, such as emails, phone numbers, or hashes, are automatically discarded rather than sent.

Can I earn Brave Rewards for opting in to Web Discovery Project?

In the future, we may offer BAT to those who opt in to the Brave Discovery Project. However, there are some fraud concerns to work out first, so we have not yet implemented this. We hope to have updates on this soon.

Where can I find source code and more technical detail about the Web Discovery Project?

  • An overview of the Web Discovery Project can be found on Brave’s GitHub repo.
  • Read the top-level README.
  • View the source code.

If you spot a potential problem, please create an issue on the repo, or contact us.

Android Browser: Settings Management

How do I change or manage site permissions Android?

You can use site permissions to control what content a website can show you and which data they can access to by default.

To view and manage site settings and permissions on Android:

  1. Launch Brave on Android
  2. Tap Settings --> Site settings
  3. Tap on the permission you would like to change

Note that you can also tap All sites at the top of the page to view a list of all sites you’ve visited and what permissions are granted for them.

For a full list of each permission and what they control, please see: How do I change site permissions?

How do I change the browser theme in Brave Android?

Brave allows you to display the app in light or dark mode to suit your preference. To change the browser theme on Android:

  1. Launch Brave and tap Main menu --> Settings.
  2. Scroll down to the Display section and tap Appearance.
  3. Tap the Theme option displayed at the top of the Appearance page:

Here you will find the main theme options available.

  • System Default: Selecting this option makes the browser match whatever the theme setting is set for on your device’s OS settings. 
  • Light: Changes the browser to use “light” theme.
  • Dark: Changes the browser to use “dark” theme.

Light theme enabled

    

Dark theme enabled

  

Experimental “Night” Mode

In addition to the options above, the Appearance page also has the option to toggle on the experimental “Night Mode” option. When this option is enabled, the browser theme will be “dark” automatically and in addition, the browser will attempt to force the content of a webpage being viewed to display in a “dark theme”. 

Night mode enabled

  

It is worth noting that this particular setting may result in some web pages displaying incorrectly. This is typically because this feature works by the browser detecting colors displayed on the webpage being viewed as “light” and attempting to change or invert them to display “dark” colors instead. However, depending on the color values used on the site, an inverted value of a particular color may not actually be ideal for viewing that content. For example, a site with a white background and gray text may get inverted to display a black background with dark-gray text, resulting in the content being difficult to read.

How do I enable Widevine DRM on Android?

What is Widevine?

Widevine is an optional browser component that allows you to play DRM-protected content. Websites such as Netflix, Hulu, HBO and Amazon Prime Video use it to protect their videos. For more information about Widevine in Brave, please see here.

Enabling Widevine

Widevine is disabled by default after installation. It can be enabled or disabled at any time by launching Brave, and going to Settings --> Media --> Widevine DRM:

    

Note that if you visit a website before enabling Widevine, you will see a prompt notifying you to do so before you can view the content. If you decline to enable Widevine when you see this prompt, you can still enable it any time in Settings as described above.

Selecting Allow (Relaunch Now) in the prompt enables the Widevine option while selecting Block in the prompt will keep Widevine disabled until it’s changed in Settings.

Minimum system requirements

For most modern DRM content, users need at least Android N, hardware support of Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), and an OEM/unmodified OS to get Widevine L1 level.

You can learn more about WidevineCdm and view the documentation on our GitHub.

How do I import or export data in Brave Android?

Outside of using Brave Sync, the Android version of Brave browser has limited import/export functionality. At this time, these actions are limited to importing and/or exporting bookmarks saved in the browser, or exporting (only) saved password data from the browser. For users wanting to move more types of data to from their mobile devices, please consider using Brave Sync instead.

How to Import or Export bookmarks

To export bookmarks from Brave on Android:

  1. Launch Brave and tap Main menu --> Bookmarks

  2. Tap the overflow menu (three dots icon) on the top right:

  3. Select Export Bookmarks:

Your bookmarks will be exported as an HTML file on your device. Use the device file explorer to move the file to the desired location.

To import a bookmarks .html file into Brave on Android:

  1. Launch Brave and tap Main menu --> Bookmarks
  2. Tap the overflow menu (three dots icon) on the top right
  3. Select Import bookmarks:

Find the bookmarks .html file on your device you would like to import. Note that you can import any bookmarks .html file into Brave – it does not have to be an .html file exported from Brave specifically, which allows you to export bookmarks from other browsers and import them into Brave.

How to export passwords in Brave on Android

To export password data from Brave on Android:

  1. Launch Brave and tap Main menu --> Brave Password Manager

  2. Tap the overflow menu (three dots icon) on the top right:

  3. Select Export passwords...:

This will export your saved passwords to your device as a .csv file.

How do I manage autofill settings Android?

When entering information in a text form, Brave may ask if you want that information to be remembered. If allowed, Brave will offer to autofill forms online if the information requested had been saved previously.

To manage saved form information:

  1. Launch Brave on your Android device
  2. Tap Main menu --> Settings
  3. Scroll down to the Autofill section of the page

Here, you can adjust autofill settings as well as add, remove or edit saved information.

Manage autofill settings for Payments

Tapping on Payment methods allows you to adjust the browser’s autofill settings for credit card information saved in the browser. 

  • Save and fill payment methods: Toggling this option “on” tells the browser to automatically fill online payment forms with saved credit card information while browser. When this option is off, credit card information will not autofill in payment forms.
  • Manually verify every time you pay using autofill: Toggling this option “on” cause the browser to prompt you to enter your device system PIN, password or fingerprint (whatever method you use to unlock your device) before the browser autofills the form with your saved credit card data. Note that, as an extra security measure, even with this option off, you will still occasionally be prompted to enter your system login after a certain amount of time before the browser autofills the form.
  • Save security codes: Toggling this option “on” will save the CVC code (typically located on the back of most credit cards) in addition to the other credit card information for faster checkouts. With this option toggled “off”, you will need to manually enter the CVC information once the rest of the form has been filled. 

Manually adding credit card information

When you enter your credit card information to make a purchase in Brave online, you will be prompted to save that information in the browser (assuming you have Save and fill payment methods toggled “on”). Alternatively, you can manually save credit card information in the browser by tapping the Add card option on the Payment methods page.

Manage autofill settings for Addresses and other form data

Tapping the Addresses and more option allows you to adjust autofill options and add, remove or edit saved form data.

Here, you can see a list of form data saved in the the browser. Toggling the Save and fill addresses option tells the browser to autofill form data with saved shipping addresses, phone numbers, email addresses. You can tap on any entry in the list to edit the saved data. Similar to the password entries mentioned above, you can add addresses and other form data by entering it into form fields while browsing and tapping Save when prompted by the browser or you can manually add an address by tapping the Add address button on this page.

How do I manage Cookies and Site data in Brave on Android?

Cookie Default Settings

There are three different cookie settings, all of which can be controlled via Brave’s Shields, or by navigating to Settings --> Site Settings --> Third-party cookies.

Allow all cookies, Block third-party cookies, Block all cookies.

Block third-party cookies is the default cookie setting. This setting allows sites that use first-party cookies to function —  for example, some sites use first party cookies to log into a site — while at the same time, it prevents ads or third party cookies from tracking your browsing activity.

Some sites may break from blocking all cookie content. Therefore in some cases you may need to enable Allow all cookies. 

How to view site data stored in Brave

To view data stored by sites visited in Brave:

  1. Launch Brave and tap Menu --> Settings
  2. Scroll down to the General section and tap Site settings
    • Here, you can view and change the default permissions allowed for sites you visit as well
  3. At the top of this menu, tap All Sites
    • Note that, alternatively, you can scroll to the bottom of this menu and tap Data stored in the Content section as well.

    

From here, you can see a list of all sites you’ve visited that have stored data. Tapping on a site in the list will show more detailed information about what the site stored.

How to delete data for individual sites

You can delete individual site data from the All Sites (or Data stored) menu, as well as from the address bar in the browser. To delete data for individual sites from the All Sites menu:

  1. To the right of each website on the All Sites menu is a “trash” icon - tapping this icon will delete all stored browsing data related to this site.

  2. If you tap on one of the sites listed in this menu for the detailed view of what is stored, you can delete individual cookies associated with the site, using the trash icon next to the data. Additionally, you can delete all site data stored by the site by tapping the Delete data & reset permissions button at the bottom of the screen:

        

  3. If you are currently viewing the website, you can tap the “tune” icon to the left of the URL in the address bar, then tap Cookies and site data, which will land you on the same site menu shown above:

        

How to delete all browsing data

To delete data stored by all sites in the browser, or all of a particular type of data for all sites:

  1. Launch Brave and tap Menu --> Settings --> Brave Shields and Privacy

  2. Scroll down to the Clear browsing data section and tap Delete browsing data - here you can see the check list of data types you can select to be deleted, along with the time range in which you want data to be deleted:

        

  3. Tap the check box next to each data type you would like to delete and select the time range for how far back you would like this data to be deleted (to delete everything, select All Time)

  4. Tap the Delete data button to complete the process. Note that this action cannot be undone.

How to delete site data “on exit”

There are also options for users who would like to clear site data automatically (that is, without having to go into settings and use the options discussed above). Brave can be configured to automatically delete all browsing data once the application is closed on your device. To do this:

  1. Launch Brave and tap Menu --> Settings --> Brave Shields and Privacy
  2. Scroll down to the Clear browsing data section and toggle the Clear data on exit option “on” (to the right, as shown below):

Note that enabling this option will automatically delete all browsing data when the Brave app is closed. Additionally, this will only trigger if the application is fully closed - simply minimizing the browser or switching to another app on your device will not cause the browser to delete data.

How to delete data for a site when the site is closed

Enabling the Forget me when I close this site option will tell the browser to clear any data that would normally be saved on a specific website once you close that tab. This is a Shields option and can be enabled on a per-site basis by opening the Shields panel while on the site, tapping Advanced controls then toggling the Forget me when I close this site option “on” (left image below).

Alternatively, this option can be enabled by default, such that it is enabled for all sites until specified otherwise by going to Settings --> Brave Shields & Privacy and toggling Forget me when I close this site “on” (right image below). 

        

Manage site data with Shields

Brave Shields also offers additional options for controlling what data gets stored, blocked, or cleared while browsing. For more information on how to use Shields to control your data, please see How do I use Shields while browsing?

How do I set Brave as my default browser Android?

💡Note: the exact steps taken to reach the default app settings may vary based on the specific Android device you’re using, but should be similar. Steps here are shown using a Samsung Galaxy device, running Android 15 and One UI v7.0

Setting Brave as your default browser in the Brave app

After installing Brave on your Android device, you can tap the main menu and select the Set as Default browser option:

Setting Brave as the default browser using you’re Android’s System settings

  1. Open your Android device’s Settings

  2. Find and tap on the Apps option

  3. On the Apps page, find and tap on the Choose Default Apps option

  4. Tap the Browser App option and select Brave from the list of installed browsers on your device

You’re all set! Brave should now be the default browser used when tapping links or viewing webpage content on your device.

How do I use the built-in password manager in Brave Android?

When you enter new login information on a website, Brave may ask if you want to save that login for the next time you visit that site. Tapping Save on the prompt displayed at the top of screen once you login to a site will save the login data for that site into the built-in password manager.

Tapping on the “gear” icon shows additional options, allowing you to select Never for this site, which will prevent the browser from prompting you again when you enter login data for that particular site. You can also use the Edit password option to quickly access and change the information entered.

    

Managing saved passwords

You can view and managed passwords saved in the browser by opening the Main menu then tapping Settings --> Brave Password manager:

Here, you can view all your saved passwords. There are a couple toggles at the top of the page you can use to configure password behavior in the browser:

  • Save Passwords: Toggling this option on/off will allow or prevent the browser from prompting you to save login information in the browser.
  • Auto Sign-in: Toggling this option on will tell the browser to automatically sign you into sites (if not signed in already) that have login information saved in the browser. If this option is “off”, you will need to re-enter this information when you go to login. Note that with autofill enabled, you will still be able to quickly enter this information into the required fields using the saved login data. 

Tapping on a password entry on this page allows you to view, copy, edit or delete password data for that site. To edit your password information, simply tap into the text field to begin editing.

  • You can delete the entry by tapping the “trash” icon on the top-right of the screen.
  • You can copy the username or password to the device clipboard by tapping the “copy” button to the right of the relevant field.
  • You can view/reveal the saved password by tapping the “eye” icon in the password field.

Note that you will be prompted to enter your device system password, fingerprint or PIN (depending on what password method used to unlock your device) to in order to reveal the saved browser password.

Brave Origin

How do I activate my Brave Origin purchase on a new device?

Once you have purchased Brave Origin, you may use it multiple times across your devices.

In order to activate your purchase on additional devices, you will need to set up a Brave Premium account which will serve as a hub for all your Brave Premium purchases. Please visit and create an account or log in to your existing account.

Please note that purchasing Brave Origin on a mobile device does not automatically create a Brave account for you. Additionally, if you have created a Brave Premium account, your mobile purchase is still completely separate from your account. In other words, these two things — your Brave Premium account and an Origin purchase made through the App Store or Play Store — are not connected until the linking process outlined below is successfully completed.

  • Activate mobile purchase to another device
  • Activate desktop purchase to another device

I’ve purchased Brave Origin on my mobile device - how do I activate Origin on other devices?

After purchasing Brave Origin on your mobile device, you can use the steps outlined below to link your purchase to your Brave Premium account. This will generate an Origin Purchase ID, which can be used to activate Brave Origin on your other devices.

For users who purchased Brave Origin on Android:
  1. Launch Brave on your Android device
  2. Navigate to Settings > Brave Origin
  3. Scroll down and tap Link purchase to your Brave account in the Purchase section of the page.
  4. You will then be redirected to account.brave.com – please login in Braveon your Android device, then tap Link my purchase to add your Brave Origin purchase to your Brave account. 

Your Brave Origin purchase should now be visible on your Brave Premium account page, along with the generated Purchase ID. You can now download Brave Origin on additional devices, and use this Purchase ID when prompted to activate Origin on that device.

For users who purchased Brave Origin on iOS:
  1. Launch Brave on your iOS device
  2. Navigate to Menu > All Settings > Brave Origin
  3. Scroll down and tap Link purchase to your Brave account in the Purchase section of the page
  4. You will then be redirected to account.brave.com – please login in Braveon your iOS device, then tap Link my purchase to add your Brave Origin purchase to your Brave account. 

I’ve purchased Brave Origin on desktop - how do I activate Origin on other devices?

After purchasing Brave Origin on a desktop device, you should be able to see Brave Origin listed on your Premium account page, which includes a unique Purchase ID. When you download and install Brave Origin on another desktop device, simply use this Purchase ID when prompted to activate Origin on that device.

If you would like to use Brave Origin on a mobile device:

  1. Launch Brave  on your mobile device
  2. Navigate to Settings > Brave Origin
  3. Tap Get a login code – you will be redirected to account.brave.com. Please enter the same email address associated with the Premium account in which you originally used to purchase Brave Origin
  4. Tap the login link sent to your email and ensure that it opens in Brave browser. Tap Link my purchase now.

Your browser will detect the Origin purchase associated with your account and automatically upgrade your browser to Origin.

How do I extend activations for Brave Origin?

There is technically no limit to the number of times you can activate Origin across your devices and platforms, but there is a monthly rate limit. Brave Origin users will see the option to add more activations on their Premium account page.

How to request more Origin activations

  1. Login to account.brave.com. Click on the option to Request more activations shown under your Brave Origin purchase.

 

  1. Additional Brave Origin activations are enabled. 

  2. Once processed, you will see Ready to activate under your Brave Origin card. Click Refresh Brave Origin on the device you wish to activate.

Troubleshooting Error Messages

Recent activation request: To prevent abuse, self-serve activations are rate limited. You can request new activations every 30 days.

Still having trouble with Brave Origin activations? Please submit a request to Brave Premium support and we can assist.

What are the differences between the Standalone and Upgradeable versions of Brave Origin?

Brave Origin is a paid version of the browser for users who don’t need all of the features that Brave offers, but still want the privacy that only Brave offers.

Brave Origin users will continue to benefit from our industry-leading privacy, ad-block, and speed (via Brave Shields), along with regular software updates, Chromium patches, and ongoing security and privacy improvements.

Brave Origin is available in two ways:

  • As a new, standalone browser product, available via a separate app download on your device.
  • As an upgrade to the existing version of Brave on your device.

Standalone vs. Upgrade Comparison

Depending on your needs, you might prefer the separate app experience or the seamless transition of upgrading your current browser. Here is how they compare:

  • Feature: Brave Origin (Standalone App) Brave Origin (Upgrade Path)
  • Installation: Requires a separate download and installation. Operates as a completely distinct app. Applied directly to your existing Brave installation. No new app needed.
  • Feature Management: Compiled Out: Non-core features are physically removed from the browser code. Toggled Off: Non-core features are disabled and hidden via internal group policy.
  • Affected Features: Leo, News, Rewards, VPN, Wallet, Talk, Playlist, Speedreader, Stats/P3A, Tor, Wayback Machine, and Web Discovery Project are automatically removed. The same features are toggled off by default, but can be re-enabled individually through the Origin settings panel.
  • Settings Panel: None. Features simply do not exist in the browser UI or code. A new Brave Origin menu appears in Settings to manage feature toggles.
  • Admin Policies: Not affected. Since features aren’t present, they cannot be forced on by IT admins. Managed device policies can override your local Origin toggles.

For Brave Origin users who download the separate, standalone app, all of the features listed above will be automatically removed. Any new features we release (outside the core of Brave Shields) would not appear in the standalone Brave Origin app. The features will be compiled out of the build.

Brave Origin users who opt to upgrade the existing Brave app on their device will see a new Settings panel. The features listed above will appear in this Settings panel, and be toggled off by default. Any new features we release outside the core of Brave Shields will appear in this panel, and also be off by default. In this case, Brave manages group policies internally to disable features.

What is Brave Origin?

Brave Origin is a minimalist version of Brave that allows users to disable the revenue-generating features that otherwise support Brave as a business. Brave Origin is available in two ways:

  • As a new, standalone browser product, available via a separate app download on your device
  • As an upgrade to the existing version of Brave on your device

Both versions will be available via a one-time purchase at , and a single purchase will give you access to both options. For example, after making this one-time purchase, you could choose to download the standalone app and upgrade your existing version of Brave, or use only one of these options.

Purchasing will provide a purchase ID that can be activated on multiple devices, in either—or a combination of both—standalone and upgrade modes. There is technically no limit to the number of times you can activate Origin across your devices and platforms, but there is a monthly rate limit. You can easily manage your activations—and request more—using self-serve controls in .

What features are affected by Brave Origin?

Brave Origin users will continue to benefit from our industry-leading privacy, adblock, and speed (via Brave Shields), as well as regular software updates, Chromium patches, and security and privacy improvements. Beyond this core, Brave Origin will affect the following features:

  • Leo
  • News
  • Playlist (iOS and desktop Nightly and Beta)
  • Rewards (which also disables browser-based Brave Ads)
  • Speedreader
  • The daily usage ping, crash logs, and privacy-preserving product analytics (P3A)
  • Talk
  • Tor
  • VPN
  • Wallet (which also disables Web3 domains)
  • Wayback Machine
  • Web Discovery Project
  • Email aliases (currently in Nightly build for desktop)

For Brave Origin users who download the separate, standalone app, all of the features listed above will be automatically removed. Any new features we release (outside the core of Brave Shields) would not appear in the standalone Brave Origin app. The features are compiled out of the build.

Brave Origin users who opt to upgrade the existing Brave app on their device will see a new Settings panel. The features listed above will appear in this Settings panel, and be toggled off by default. Any new features we release outside the core of Brave Shields will appear in this panel, and also be off by default. In this case, Brave manages group policies internally to disable features.

How to access Brave Origin

Brave Origin is available via one-time purchase, but the standalone and upgrade versions have different availability on different operating systems. Brave Origin is also available for free for Linux users. The table below should clarify the options:  

  • Available as an upgrade

    Available as a standalone app

    Available as a one-time purchase

    Available for free

  • Android (1.91.x and above): ✅ ✅

  • iOS (1.91.x and above): ✅ ✅

  • macOS (1.91.x and above): ✅ ✅ ✅

  • Windows  (1.91.x and above): ✅ ✅ ✅

  • Linux  (1.91.x and above): ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Note that while Brave Origin is available as a free download for Linux users, these users are of course still welcome to purchase if they’d like to support Brave.

How to use Brave Origin as a standalone app (desktop only)
  1. Download Brave Origin for your desktop device.
  2. Complete the installation, and open the Brave Origin app.
    • You’ll be presented with prompts to either verify your purchase or buy now on the Brave Premium account site.
  3. If you haven’t yet done so, complete your purchase. Be sure to save the purchase ID you receive.
  4. Go back to the Brave Origin app and enter this purchase ID.
  5. Complete the onboarding flow, and browse as you normally would.

Linux users can choose to skip the purchase process and get the Brave Origin standalone app for free. To do so, they should download and install Brave Origin, then click the Proceed with Origin for free on Linux button. Note that this dialog appears only once on Linux.

Also note that the standalone version of Brave Origin will have its own Nightly, Beta, and Release channels, distinct from the free (or Brave Origin-upgraded) Brave channels.

How to use Brave Origin as an upgrade

If you opt to use Brave Origin as an upgrade to the existing Brave app on your device, you’ll see a new control panel in the Brave Settings menu. Existing features—as well as any new features we ship in the future—would appear here, and be toggled off by default.

To upgrade on desktop:

  1. Click “☰” (Settings), click System, and scroll to Brave Origin.
  2. If you haven’t yet purchased Brave Origin, click Buy now. You will be taken to the Brave Premium account site.
    • If you’ve already purchased Brave Origin, and you’d like to upgrade Brave on another device, log in to the Brave Premium account site to get your log-in code.
  3. Complete your purchase. Be sure to save the purchase ID you receive if you’d like to use the standalone build as well.
  4. Click Refresh Origin on the account page. The Brave browser will restart.
  5. Open the main Settings menu again, and click Brave Origin.
  6. You should now see the panel where you can toggle features on / off.

If you upgrade to Brave Origin and later decide you don’t want to use it, you can downgrade the installation back to the original standard Brave by going to brave://flags/#brave-origin and changing the value of this flag to Disabled. Note that this will require a browser relaunch before taking affect.

Note that Linux users can choose to skip the purchase process and upgrade to Brave Origin for free by clicking Proceed with Origin for free on Linux on the desktop Settings page.

To upgrade on mobile:

  1. Tap “⋮” (Android) or “…” (iOS), tap All Settings, scroll to General, and tap Brave Origin.
  2. If you haven’t yet purchased Brave Origin, tap Buy now. You will be taken to the Play Store or App Store.
    • If you’ve already purchased Brave Origin, and you’d like to upgrade Brave on another device, click Get a Login Code instead.
  3. Restart the Brave app.
  4. Open the main Settings menu again, and tap Brave Origin.
  5. You should now see the panel where you can toggle features on / off.

How Brave Origin maintains user privacy

Some early Brave Origin users have asked how Brave can maintain user privacy while requiring a purchase ID (either from a Brave premium account or from the App Store / Play Store).

Brave uses a blind token protocol based on Privacy Pass, which decouples payment identity from service usage. These privacy-preserving subscription credentials allow the browser to verify you have a valid purchase of a premium product (like Brave Origin) without learning anything about you.

Using Brave Origin in a workplace or managed-device setting

Brave Origin will add admin policies for every Brave Origin-related feature. This means that if you use Brave and purchase Brave Origin on a workplace device managed through Group Policy, your administrator could decide to enable or disable certain features, which would override your local device Brave Origin settings.

For example if your admin decided to enable Brave VPN for everyone in your work group, you would still see the VPN icon in the browser even if you had initially disabled Brave VPN in the Brave Origin settings panel. Likewise, if your admin decided to disable Brave VPN for everyone in your work group, you would not see the icon in the browser even if you had initially enabled it in the Brave Origin settings panel. In other words, admin policies will override your local Brave Origin settings.

Note: This is only applicable to Brave Origin as an upgrade.

Brave Rewards: Brave Ads

Brave Ads FAQ

Below is a list of commonly asked questions related to the Brave Ads.

How are “Brave Ads” different from ads I see while browsing in other browsers, and why would I want to see them?

There are some key differences between Brave Ads and traditional digital advertising:

  1. Brave Ads are privacy-preserving. Traditional advertising requires information about you, your behavior, your browsing history, location, and more, to be collected by advertisers in order for them to target their ads to you. In contrast, when a Brave Ad is matched to you, it is done on your own device, by your own device, inside Brave itself. Your personal data never leaves your own device.

  2. You can earn and get paid. By enabling Brave Rewards, you can earn Basic Attention Token (BAT) for the Brave Ads you see. You can then use your BAT to buy gift cards, send to content creators, exchange for other currencies (both fiat and crypto), and more.

  3. Brave Ads don’t get in the way of content. There are different kinds of Brave Ads you can choose to see. For example, there are notification ads and background images on the New Tab Page. You can find a list of the different ad formats here. Unlike traditional ads, Brave Ads don’t get in the way of content you’re trying to watch (like traditional video ads or commercials) or read online (like banner ads).

     

Do Brave Ads track or collect my data in any way?

Brave uses anonymous-but-accountable ad confirmation events to allow us to report campaign performance and delivery for advertisers without tracking users and without personal data leaving the user’s device. Additional technical information about the security and privacy model used for ad confirmation is available on GitHub. In addition to accounting via confirmations, it is important to gain anonymous insights into how Brave users engage with ads, e.g. with respect to top-level advertising segments like “Technology & Computing” or “Travel”.

To that end we use privacy-preserving analytics that allow us to calculate high-level statistics about ad usage without gaining insight into any information about particular individual users. To learn about how we achieve this read our posts on Privacy Preserving Product Analytics and Private Advertising Analytics.

How does Brave determine my region for Brave Ads?

The region/country setting for Brave Ads is inferred by Fastly on the edge using the IP address of the ad catalog request.

How long do I have to view the ad before my “attention” accounts as a “view”?

You are rewarded for merely having a Brave Ad appear on your screen. You don’t need to click or engage with it if you don’t want to. However, if you’re interested in an ad and what it has to offer, you should definitely click on the ad.

What if I’m served an ad that is offensive or inappropriate?

Please email .

Also, note that you can manage which Brave Ads you see by going into your browser settings. If you have Brave Rewards enabled, then you can easily manage which Brave Ads you see by going into your Brave Rewards settings page at brave://rewards. 

Ads themselves can often gather data or contain harmful content or lead to malware. How does Brave filter out “bad actors” from the ads served?

There are several ways we prevent harmful ads from ever being served on the platform:

  1. Third-party ads require data collection in order to function as expected. Brave blocks third party ads and trackers, including ad exchanges and networks that commonly deliver malware and malvertising.
  2. The same Brave Shields that protect users as they browse the web are active when you open up a webpage via a Brave Ad.
  3. Advertisers are required to go through an approval process before they are able to set up campaigns with Brave.

Are Brave Ads available in my region?

A full list of regions where Brave Ads are running can be found on

Please note that ad campaigns vary by country, and by operating system. In some countries, there may be fewer ads observed throughout the month based on campaign size, delivery pacing, operating systems, content categories and that advertisers have selected to run their ads to. As we continue to generate additional demand for countries where Brave Ads are available, the consistency should improve over time.

 

I set notification ads to display ‘X’ ads an hour. Why am I not receiving ‘X’ ads per hour?

Please note that this setting is a ceiling rather than a floor. That is, it does not dictate how many ads you are guaranteed to  see per hour, but the maximum number of notifications Brave is allowed to show you per hour. This number will always fall between 0 and X, inclusive.

Why are many of the Brave Ads I’m seeing crypto-focused?

Many crypto-related companies like advertising through Brave because of its audience, and Brave’s openness to Web3. Additionally, some Brave Ads are matched to your interests. So, if you’re someone who’s interested in crypto, you may see more crypto-focused advertisements.

Do you need to click on Brave Ads to earn BAT?

You do not need to click or press on Brave Ads in order to earn from them. You earn BAT for Brave Ads when they appear on your screen. For example, when a Brave Ads push notification appears on your screen, you earn for just having it appear on your screen. However, you should certainly click a Brave Ad if you’re interested in the ad and would like to learn more about what it has to offer.

If you’d like to dismiss a Brave Ads push notification without opening it, you can swipe or slide it away. If you don’t engage with it, the push notification will automatically disappear after a couple of minutes.

There are different kinds of Brave Ads (ad formats) that you’ll experience. You can learn more here.

Please see this guide on how to configure ads.

New Tab Page Ads Reporting

This article covers the way we measure ad performance for New Tab Page Sponsored images and how Brave keeps that information anonymous and private.

What are sponsored images?

Sponsored images are full-page visual ads that appear as the background image on newly opened tabs in Brave. They either promote a Brave product or service, or those of an advertiser.

These ads are a privacy-first way for advertisers to raise awareness of their brand and products, and for Brave to earn revenue. This revenue allows Brave to continue offering its products for free to everyone.

How does Brave ensure anonymity with ad reporting?

In order to protect your privacy, and ensure ad views / ad engagement cannot be tied to an individual, we send reporting requests through a proxy that hides your IP address.

This ensures Brave will not have enough information to determine who you are (not that we even want to), either as an individual or as a singled-out member of the group of users sending a report to our server. Additionally, we can’t tell that two reports about two different ads are coming from the same person. This is by design, as we have no need for this information. Essentially, Brave has only a count of Brave users who interacted with an ad, but not enough information about these users to single them out from everyone else.

What data do you collect when I interact with new tab page ads?

In order to help advertisers measure the impact of their advertising, and decide whether to spend more with Brave in the future, we provide advertisers with an aggregate report of how Brave users as a group interact with their ads.

This report includes:

  • How many users saw their ad
  • How many users clicked their ad

Producing this report requires us to send an anonymous report from your browser to Brave’s servers whenever you view or click on such an ad. This in turn allows us to determine:

  • Which ad was involved
  • The country you are coming from (derived from your IP address)
  • Your browser version
  • Your operating system (e.g. Windows or Android)

How can I opt out of sponsored images?

  • Desktop
  • Android
  • iOS

To opt out of seeing these new tab page ads on a desktop device, you can disable sponsored images from the Customize menu on the new tab page.

To opt out of seeing these new tab page ads on an Android device:

  1. Tap “⋮” then Settings
  2. Tap New Tab Page
  3. Tap Show Sponsored Images

To opt out of seeing these new tab page ads on an iOS device:

  1. Tap “…” Settings
  2. Tap All Settings
  3. Tap New Tab Page
  4. Tap Media Type
  5. Toggle to Default Images

FAQ

How long is Brave Ads data stored in my browser?

Sponsored images data is stored locally (i.e. on your device) for two days. This ensures Brave can send the information anonymously to our servers regardless of network conditions.

Is Brave Ads data stored in private windows?

No. Sponsored images do not appear in private/Tor windows, so there’s no Brave Ads data to collect from browsing sessions conducted in these windows.

Can I see what sponsored images my browser interacted with?

Yes. You can see the sponsored images your browser has interacted with by visiting brave://ads-internals. These are labeled as new_tab_page_ad.

Can I delete this information?

Yes, you can delete this information from your browser. To do so, visit brave://settings/clearBrowserData and click Clear Brave Ads data. The information will then be removed from your device.

What are Brave Survey Panels?

A survey panel is a group of individuals who have agreed to participate in research studies. For users who opt-in to join a survey panel, Brave may present opportunities to participate in surveys. 

How does participation in the survey panel help Brave?

Brave surveys fall into two general categories:

  • Surveys that can demonstrate to advertisers whether their privacy-first sponsored image campaign was successful for raising awareness of their products. (This in turn helps Brave earn revenue.)
  • Surveys to capture user feedback and market research about Brave and its products. This feedback helps us ensure we’re building the features that users want. 

What data do you collect when I participate in a survey panel? How long is the data kept?

For surveys related to Brave’s advertising campaigns, we will retain some on-device, campaign-level ad metrics for up to 90 days. These metrics are used to ensure that the surveys are only sent to users who have seen or clicked on the associated ads.

If you choose to respond to a survey about Brave or its products, we will retain your responses for up to 1 year.

Our survey platform does not log IP addresses.

While most A/V software does not interfere with Brave Ads, at this time it is known that users running Kaspersky Internet Security may not see ads appear while the application is running. To configure Kaspersky to allow Brave Ads to show while running:

  1. Launch Kaspersky on your system
  2. Go to Settings --> Network settings
  3. Scroll down to Encrypted connection scanning
  4. Select the Do not scan encrypted connections option
  5. Click save, relaunch Brave
